title: Vayeshev: the man in the field (Genesis 37:15–17)
hookLine: a nameless stranger points Joseph to his brothers; midrash calls him an angel

cards: You're lost in a new city. Your phone is dead. You've walked the same block three times.
Then someone, an old man at a bus stop, a kid on a bike, asks: you look lost, where are you trying to go? Two sentences later you're on your way, and you never see them again.
Joseph's brothers are far from home, grazing the flocks. Jacob sends Joseph, alone, to check on them. He goes to Shechem, where they were supposed to be.

teach.b: The Torah says a man found Joseph wandering in the field. Just, a man. No name.
He asks, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "What seekest thou?" Joseph answers, in Hebrew: et achai anochi mevakesh.
"I seek my brethren." Tell me, please, where they're pasturing. The stranger says: they've moved on.

I heard them say, let's go to Dothan. So Joseph goes to Dothan, the brothers see him coming, and the story turns. The pit, the caravan, Egypt: everything that follows starts with a stranger who knew where they'd gone.
Why does the Torah bother with him? Three verses for a man with no name, who asks one question and gives one answer. The commentators each give an answer.
An old midrash, which Rashi quotes, says the man was the angel Gabriel.
Ramban, in medieval Spain, said: whether or not he was an angel, the point is that Joseph's story had to happen, and when Joseph was about to give up and go home, someone was put in his path.
Others read him as simply a passerby, which may be the point too. The text itself doesn't say who he was. It only tells us that when Joseph was lost, somebody noticed, asked, and pointed.
A life can have figures like that too. A teacher who mentioned a book. A stranger who gave a name, a number, a direction.
Their names slip away, and the thanks go unsaid.

how: Joseph's words, et achai anochi mevakesh, I seek my brothers, are quoted in Jewish teaching and song as a call to look for and care for one another.

o: and he settled, the portion of Joseph's story
and he wandered, Joseph lost in the field
and he sought, for 'I seek my brothers'

games.q: who did what in the field — tap the pairs.
p: sent Joseph to check on his brothers

s: the Torah names the man in the field
he's just 'a man'; the text never tells us who he was.
an old midrash, quoted by Rashi, says the man was an angel
it names him as the angel Gabriel.
the brothers were where Jacob thought they'd be
they had moved on from Shechem to Dothan.

games.q: you're Joseph, alone in a field near Shechem. your brothers aren't here. a stranger asks, what are you looking for? what do you say?
games.why: Joseph said, I seek my brethren. the man told him they'd gone to Dothan, and the story turned.

practice: Think back to a time you were lost, in a city, a job, a hard year, and to someone who pointed the way, whether or not you knew their name. Picture their face if you can, and silently say thank you.
If you pray, you can thank God for putting them in your path.

wordCard.voice: Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion where a nameless man in a field points Joseph to his brothers, and the whole story turns.

orig.note: Hebrew: I seek my brothers. Joseph's answer to the man in the field.

carryVoice: Your line: someone points the way. Even a man with no name. Day two hundred two, done.
